allowlist.reason: Hardware check: reads /proc/meminfo for system stats

Daemon-reachability boundary: this module forwards MCP tool calls to the daemon, which is the graph authority. Every filesystem touch here is about reaching that authority, never about answering in its place — no tool result derives from any of them. Three classes, each pinned to its whole expression: (1) the loopback bearer token at <kin_dir>/daemon.token, read so the forwarded request can authenticate; (2) repo binding, walking up from the working directory for the .kin layout marker to locate that token, which precedes any graph consult because it decides which daemon to talk to; (3) revival, resolving and spawning the known kin-daemon executable via KIN_DAEMON_BIN, the current exe's directory, the cargo target dir, and PATH, a `which` equivalent open-coded to avoid the dependency. The head-generation marker is the daemon's own published counter and only keys a within-session memo; a missing marker reads as generation 0, which costs cross-generation invalidation and never substitutes for a graph answer. Pinned rather than whole-file so any newly added filesystem primitive or subprocess in this module fails the guard The revival wait is split into its own helper so the spawned child handle outlives every exit it can take and reaches the detached-daemon reaper exactly once; its `&mut std::process::Child` parameter is process-lifecycle plumbing with no answer surface.

Config/capability IO: probes the local model cache directory for reranker availability now and for whether this install ever fetched the model; never reads repo content and is not a semantic answer path

Config/capability IO over the local embedding-model cache, the same root retrieval_profile.rs probes for the reranker. This module mirrors the loader's own cache layout to say whether the runtime embedding-model download has happened, is in flight, or will never happen: it tests whether a KIN_EMBED_MODEL_ID names a local directory, because such an id short-circuits the hub fetch and reporting it as a pending download would announce egress that never happens, and it walks the model's cache directory to sum the bytes already there, skipping symlinked snapshot entries so a resolved snapshot is never counted twice and bounded by a fixed entry budget. Those bytes are the numerator of a progress line on init, resources inspect, graph status and doctor; nothing here reads repository content and no result of it feeds locate, search, context, trace, review, xref, or rename. Pinned by exact expression so any newly added filesystem primitive in this module fails the guard until it is re-justified.

Telemetry consent boundary: the only filesystem touch in the locate authority path is the presence of the consent marker, which gates telemetry and never contributes to the ranked answer. Pinned so any other filesystem primitive in this module fails the guard

Known violation under repair, not a boundary claim. Unlike every other entry here, these reads ARE the answer authority: `kin spec list` and `kin spec show` resolve their result by walking and parsing .kin/specs/*.json, which is exactly what the Zero File-Search Authority Rule forbids on a query path. The entry exists so the violation is visible, owned, and dated rather than invisible, which it was until this module entered the scanned query set: nothing had ever reported it. It is not evidence the path is graph-backed and must not be read as one. The reason it cannot simply be fixed is storage, not wiring: the pinned registry crates carry no home for a spec. kin_model::Spec is a bare data struct, GraphStore composes EntityStore, ChangeStore, WorkStore, ReviewStore, VerificationStore, ProvenanceStore and SessionStore and none of them has a spec method, and kin-db imports SpecId without using it. Mapping a spec onto a WorkItem would drop constraints, affected systems, validation requirements and the free-string scope, so the faithful fix is a SpecStore in kin-model and kin-db, which is a bottom-up registry publish. Tracked on the internal board for the command and for the store substrate; both pins and this entry come out when the query path reads graph truth. Pinned to the seven exact expressions rather than the whole file, so the debt cannot grow: any newly added filesystem primitive in this module fails the guard

Repository selection boundary: resolves symlinks on a repository root so a client-supplied workspace root and the process working directory compare equal when they name the same repo (/tmp against /private/tmp on macOS, tempdirs under /var/folders in fixtures). It decides which repository to bind, before a binding exists and before any graph is consulted, so it precedes the answer path rather than serving it: no file contents are read and no query result derives from it. The error case falls back to the path as given rather than treating failure as absence, so it is not an existence probe. Pinned to the whole expression, so a bare canonicalize that did read failure as a signal, or any other filesystem primitive in this module, still fails the guard

Install-diagnostic boundary: kin health reports on the local installation, so the environment is its subject rather than a source of semantic answers. The line this pin enforces is that environment probes are a diagnostic boundary while repo-content reads are not, and every pinned expression was checked against it individually. Four classes: (1) install artifacts — the kin-daemon binary beside the current exe or in the cargo target dir, the VFS shim's metadata and its four-byte object header, the shell hook, the editor extensions directory; (2) environment config — the shell rc, of which zsh has two, since the interactive .zshrc carries the hook and the always-read .zshenv carries the PATH line, and doctor reads both so an install that put the PATH line where a non-interactive shell can see it is not reported as missing it, and the AI-client MCP configs for Claude, Cursor, Codex and Antigravity, which are read to check the kin server entry and never for their surrounding content; (3) repo binding — the layout-discovered repository root is compared against the repository argument recorded in client config, and that root is first resolved to its canonical form, because the config writers record the canonicalized path and an unresolved root makes the check reject setup's own write wherever the two forms differ, which is every Windows install (the \?\ verbatim prefix) and any symlinked ancestor. The resolution takes a path already produced by layout discovery, reads no repository content, and its result is only ever compared, never returned as an answer. The setup-ledger fingerprint check belongs to this same class: it re-reads the client config bytes setup itself wrote to prove the on-disk entry is still the recorded one, and probes the recorded repository's existence before trusting the record, both feeding a comparison and never an answer; (4) a projection audit — read_dir over .kin/runs listing session workspaces left materialized. That last one is a filesystem read by necessity rather than by shortcut: it detects materialized state that reconcile has not reclaimed, and a graph that believed those sessions closed would report nothing, which is the exact failure the check exists to catch, so the traversal audits the projection against graph truth instead of standing in for it. Semantic readiness itself comes from daemon-owned embedding state, not sidecar presence. A fifth class, host assessment: two absolute-path subprocess probes (pgrep for the syspolicyd pid, ps for its CPU share) sample the macOS binary-assessment daemon so a saturated assessor is named as the cause of machine-wide launch stalls instead of surfacing as random tool hangs; they read scheduler state about the host, never repository content, and no output feeds a semantic answer. A sixth class, severity discrimination: four probes that decide whether a check reports a failure or reports nothing wrong, each testing for the presence of an artifact rather than reading one. The kin-vfs driver beside the managed binaries separates a shim the installer deliberately removed on a host that cannot run projection from a shim missing where projection is installed. The repository's daemon endpoint record separates a repository no daemon has ever started for from one whose daemon left its record behind unreachable. A .kin entry the layout already refused separates a partial or corrupt repository from a directory that simply is not one, and it is a probe for the marker directory, never a read of anything inside it; the layout, not this probe, decides what a repository is, and it has already answered before the probe runs. The fourth resolves two paths to their canonical form so the managed toolchain directory can be recognized as itself rather than as a repository someone failed to initialize, which is the same comparison-only use as class (3) and returns no answer. None of the four reads repository source content, and each exists so a correct install stops being reported as broken. No pinned expression reads repository source content. Pinned rather than whole-file so this module is falsifiable at every site and any newly added filesystem primitive fails the guard A seventh class, driver loadability: the kin-vfs driver is resolved beside the running binary, in the managed bin directory and on PATH, and the one candidate that is a regular file is executed with --help, stdin closed, and judged on whether the process reached its own code rather than on a zero exit, because the shipped driver takes a subcommand and exits 2 on a healthy install while a loader refusal exits 127 or dies at spawn. Existence is not loadability: an archive has shipped a driver needing a newer glibc than the host carries, and only running it produces the loader's message, which doctor then reports verbatim. The probe runs a binary that is part of Kin's own install, reads nothing from any repository, and its result decides between absent, loadable and unloadable rows. The managed bin directory's presence is tested for the same diagnostic reason: doctor --fix writes a PATH line for that directory only when it exists, so the check reports which of the two cases the install is in instead of promising a PATH entry for a directory nothing populated. An eighth class, projection reach: one read of the home directory and an lstat of each of its first few entries, taken only when the shim is injected into this process, stopping at the first entry that answers. Both calls are deliberate syscalls through whatever the loader has inserted, and their subject is the projection layer rather than any repository. Every other probe this row takes is inside the repository, which is the one path an engaged shim is certain to serve, so a shim answering an error for paths under the home directory read as healthy in the same shell where git exited 128 reading $HOME/.config/git/config. The stat matters beside the read, because the observed failure was for paths under the home directory and a probe that only listed it would miss the case it exists for. It is an lstat rather than a stat, and it walks several entries rather than one, so that a dangling symlink or a file removed between the listing and the probe cannot report a healthy machine as a broken projection. Neither call reads repository content, neither result is returned as an answer, and the pair exists so the projection row stops reporting health it never measured.
Git export boundary: probes the output path's git layout to decide open-vs-init before materializing graph truth as git objects. Explicit output boundary, not a semantic answer
Git ingestion boundary: open_repo probes the .git layout before mining commit history into graph relations. Co-change relations are read back from the graph, never from this traversal
IO Boundary: notification delivery and its own suppression state; answers no semantic query and never reads repository content

Notification identity boundary; answers no semantic query and never reads repository content. The std::process:: matches outside run_action are an ExitCode import, a PID used for notification request uniqueness, and process exit. run_action is function-pinned because it is the notification action boundary: a button press runs the managed kin with a fixed argument vector chosen inside this file and never supplied by the caller, after confirming that managed binary exists. It derives nothing from what it runs and cannot serve locate, search, context, trace, review, xref, or rename.
False positive: no filesystem access; the std::process:: match is an ExitCode import for the platform dispatch stub

Daemon process-boundary module end to end: bounded compatibility probes and their process-tree containment, capture, cancellation, and cleanup. It reaches and validates the daemon that owns graph authority and never derives a semantic query answer from filesystem or subprocess output. The file is dedicated to this boundary, so a whole-file exemption is reviewable; any future answer logic belongs elsewhere and requires removing or narrowing this exemption.

Daemon process lifecycle boundary with zero answer-authority surface. The exact expression pins cover process construction, readiness records, port records, PID records, and Linux process-table inspection; each reaches or supervises the daemon that owns graph truth and never derives a semantic answer. The PID record is read to establish that a daemon is still running, which is a liveness question about a process rather than a question about repository content: it can only withhold a restart, never produce or repair an answer. ManagedInstallSpawnFence::acquire is separately function-pinned because it is an install-mutation boundary: it binds the configured executable and update lock, rejects replaced or retired install roots, and serializes daemon spawn against uninstall. It reads only install/process identity metadata and cannot answer locate, search, context, trace, review, xref, or rename. The rest of this single-module crate remains scanned, and exact pin counts make any added occurrence fail closed. The death note and the daemon-log append are the same boundary read in the other direction: a daemon ended from outside cannot log its own cause, because the reaper's SIGTERM grace is shorter than the daemon's shutdown and the SIGKILL that follows lands while the arm that would print a shutdown line is still unpolled. These write that cause into the repository the daemon served and read it back, so a failed request can name a killed daemon instead of quoting a socket error. They carry process lifecycle facts only and answer no question about repository content. The open-transaction marker is the third instance of the same lifecycle boundary: the daemon publishes the phase and last beat of a write transaction it has open into .kin/daemon.transaction, the reaper reads it to tell a busy daemon from a wedged one, and the CLI reads it, together with the durable authority receipt, to classify a commit whose reply was lost as landed, still running, or gone. The four expressions pinned for it write, read and retire that one marker; the temporary-file removal is shared with the death note, which is why its count is two. They carry process lifecycle facts only, and none of them reads repository content or feeds a semantic answer. The boot-cost record is the fourth instance of the same lifecycle boundary and the narrowest: a daemon that has just finished opening a store writes what that open cost into .kin/daemon-boot-cost.json, and the next CLI spawn reads it back to size the idle window it gives the daemon it is about to start. It exists because the process that can measure an open is not the process that needs the number, and a fixed window shorter than a store's own cold start expires the daemon between two commands so the next one pays the whole open again. The three expressions pinned for it write, retire and read that one marker under its own local name, so its counts are separate from the death note's and the transaction marker's rather than folded into them. It carries a duration and nothing else, and can only lengthen or shorten how long a daemon idles; it never reads repository content and cannot produce, rank, fill or repair an answer to locate, search, context, trace, review, xref, or rename. The approaching-commit announcement is the same boundary again, written by the client rather than by the daemon. A commit and the ambient reconcile tick both admit the whole working copy, so whichever publishes first makes the other's publication redundant, and the tick already stands down for a commit it knows about. It cannot know about the one commit that matters most here, the one that had to start the daemon, because that commit reaches its handler only after the store has opened and the first reconcile round has already decided. The client therefore writes the announcement before it does any of its own work and withdraws it on the way out, and the daemon reads it back on the round that is about to decide. It carries a pid and a timestamp and nothing else. It can only withhold one ambient publication that a commit is about to make redundant, never produce, rank, fill or repair an answer to locate, search, context, trace, review, xref, or rename, and it is bounded twice over: the record expires on its own, and a round stands down for a bounded number of consecutive rounds whatever the record says. Its four expressions are pinned under their own local name so its counts stay separate from the death note's, the transaction marker's and the boot cost's rather than folded into them. The kill record is the fifth instance of the same lifecycle boundary, and the cgroup readings are what let it say anything true. A daemon the kernel kills writes no note at all, so the reaper that already waits on every daemon this process started records the kill against the store that daemon served, and every surface that later meets a dead daemon reads it back instead of quoting a socket error. The two cgroup files it reads are the host's own memory accounting under /sys, not repository content: they say what this container's cap is and how many processes the kernel has killed inside it, sampled once before a daemon is started and again when it is found dead, because a counter read only after a death cannot say the kill it counts was this daemon's. Neither reading, and neither the write nor the read of the record itself, touches a file in the repository or feeds locate, search, context, trace, review, xref, or rename. They can only add a sentence to an error the caller was already receiving. The install-mutation fence that used to be exempt as a whole function is now pinned by expression instead, one pin per primitive, so its body is scanned again. The trade is worth making for the reason the guard's own falsification harness gives for the two bodies it reground before this one: a whole-body exemption swallows anything planted inside it, and a probe that lands there reports a blind spot the file does not otherwise have. The primitives are unchanged in what they do. They resolve the configured install root and the daemon binary to their canonical forms, refuse a symlinked or replaced root or binary, and take the update lock as a regular file, re-checking both after the lock is held so a swap during admission is caught. Every one of them reads install and process identity metadata, none reads repository content, and none can produce, rank, fill or repair an answer to locate, search, context, trace, review, xref, or rename. The sweep-interruption tally is the sixth instance of the same lifecycle boundary and the smallest: one number, written by the daemon after a sweep ends and read back by the next daemon to decide whether to queue another. It moved here from the daemon because three surfaces outside the daemon now have to say the same thing about it, and a second spelling of the same file in each of them is exactly the duplication the cgroup readers were moved down here to end. The two expressions pinned for it read and write that one file under its own local name. It carries a count and nothing else, it can only withhold an enrichment sweep or add a sentence to a report the caller was already receiving, and neither it nor anything derived from it touches repository content or feeds locate, search, context, trace, review, xref, or rename.

Daemon RPC surface. This file is the answer authority every agent, editor, and CLI reaches, so it is scanned in full and only four explicit IO-boundary bodies are excused. npm_registry_routes and router_with_auth_and_shutdown materialize package-registry directories; health reports local runtime diagnostics; ensure_loopback_token manages the loopback credential. None derives a semantic query answer. The two expression pins cover a graph-owned blob lease metadata accessor and the durable authority publication-record probe. Locate, search, context, trace, impact, review, verify, MCP handlers, and every newly added handler remain scanned by default.

Supervisor process lifecycle boundary. The supervisor owns the daemon process, not any query answer, and each excused body is one of four classes. Endpoint records: the pid and port files, written through a temp-and-rename and removed only by the process that owns them, plus the url and canonical-path helpers that read them back. Singleton locks: the lifecycle guard file and its owner stamp, which decide whether another supervisor is already live. Install and process identity: the loopback auth token, same-binary comparison against the running executable, the log length and mtime probes, re-exec of the supervisor binary, and the reaper that kills rogue daemons. Registration payload and health: the repository record sent to the control plane and the local status report. None of these reads repository content, and no query result derives from any of them. Function-scoped rather than whole-file so the rest of the module, and anything added to it, stays scanned; the single expression pin is a struct field holding the lock file handle.

Daemon lifecycle boundary: starting, finding, and stopping the process that holds graph authority. Five classes, all excused per function. Singleton coordination: the lock file, its owner stamp, and the guards that decide whether this process may become the daemon. Endpoint publication and ownership: the pid, port, and owner components are written atomically, read back, and removed only after owner-bound proof; the named ownership helpers make that proof independently testable without adding query authority. Binary resolution and liveness: locating and validating the exact kin-daemon executable and probing whether an endpoint is answering before spawning another. Bounded macOS process ownership: the private launchctl capture, stable process-group guardian, deadline, and cleanup helpers. Platform registration and migration: the digest-addressed LaunchAgent plist, exact legacy-authority inspection, staged replacement, rollback, and non-macOS no-op counterparts, which is why two public names carry a count of two. Every path here reaches, supervises, or registers the authority and answers no repository query. The expression pins are process/file handle declarations and the capture file's Drop cleanup; none produces an answer. Function-scoped so the remainder of the module stays scanned.
allow_match: use std::process::{Child, Command, ExitStatus, Output, Stdio};

allowlist.reason: Daemon state persistence boundary. The excused bodies write and read back state the daemon owns about itself, never repository content. Snapshot and marker persistence: the generation marker, the vfs version record, the mcp transaction log, and the coordination event log, each written through a temp-and-rename with an explicit directory fsync so a crash cannot leave a torn record, which is what the two cfg-gated sync_directory_metadata bodies and the two `open` bodies are. Failure accounting: the persisted failure count and its marker file. Graph-to-disk projection: staging and finalizing the canonical read index from graph truth, invalidating it, and asking whether the durable index and marker already describe the generation being loaded so startup can skip republishing bytes it would have rewritten unchanged. That reuse probe is a question about a derived artifact this same module publishes, never about repository content: it decides whether to rewrite the projection, and a false answer costs a redundant rebuild rather than a wrong answer. Authority pinning: resolving the registered local repository authority roots. The two expression pins are lease metadata accessors, which return graph-owned workspace state and only share a name with the filesystem probe. One resolves the registered sibling workspaces at startup; the other names the workspace whose semantic overlay language-server enrichment is published into, so those relations survive the process that found them. Pinned on the exact expression with a count rather than by function, so a third one, filesystem or not, fails the guard until it is justified here. Derived-sidecar disclosure: load_validated_vector_index asks kin-db to install the persisted vector index and probes for that same sidecar's presence beforehand. The probe decides nothing about the answer to any query and cannot change what the graph returns; the sidecar either installed or it did not, and kin-db reports both a missing sidecar and a rejected one as the same negative. It separates those two so a rejected index is announced as the discarded work it is instead of reading as a repository that never had one, which is the whole of FIR-1959. Nothing is read from the file, no content is recovered from it, and a probe that lied in either direction would change only the wording of a health report. Derived-coverage disclosure: record_embedding_coverage_complete, record_embedding_pass_drained, and write_embedding_coverage_marker publish a marker recording that this store's embedding fill once reached whole coverage, and embedding_coverage_ever_complete reads it back. The two recorders differ only in their evidence: one re-reads the live counters, the other is called by a pass that drained its own queue and therefore cannot lose to work admitted in the moment after, which is FIR-2203. The marker is written by the daemon that finished the fill and read only by the readiness report, which needs it to tell a store filling for the first time apart from one that held full coverage and lost it. It records a fact about work this same module did, names no entity, carries no repository content, and cannot change what any query returns; a probe that lied in either direction would change only whether a health check reads pending or stale, which is FIR-2103. Function-scoped rather than whole-file: this module is large and holds far more than its persistence paths, and all of that stays scanned.

Durable bookkeeping marker published beside the authority head, not an answer authority. The excused bodies read and write .kin/kindb/last-admission, which records when a complete exact-tree admission last succeeded and how many artifacts it covered. It is written only where an admission actually completed and read only by freshness surfaces, which is what lets `kin graph status` state how far graph truth has fallen behind instead of printing an all-clear over a store admitted months ago. The record names no entity, carries no repository content, and cannot change what any query returns: a reader that lied in either direction would change only the wording of a freshness line, never a locate, search, context, trace, review, or xref answer. Publication is a temp-and-rename with an fsync of the staged file and then of the containing directory, the same shape write_generation_marker and read_generation_marker in crates/kin-daemon/src/state.rs use for the authority head marker this sits beside, and the two cfg-gated sync_directory_metadata bodies are that directory fsync. Routing through a shared boundary helper instead was not available: kin-core exposes no public atomic-write path, and config.rs, registry.rs, and the daemon's state.rs each open-code their own. Function-scoped rather than whole-file so the rest of the module stays scanned, including the three-way read classification and the age arithmetic the surfaces render, and so any newly added filesystem primitive here fails the guard until it is justified.

Durable bookkeeping marker published beside the last-admission marker, not an answer authority. The excused bodies read and write .kin/kindb/relation-census, which records the relation-kind histogram as it stood when the graph's relations were last settled, so `kin graph status` can compare its own census to the previous one instead of printing an all-clear over a store that lost a whole relation kind. It is written only at the end of a completed enrichment sweep and at the end of a commit, never on a read path, and read only by the status and doctor surfaces. The record names no entity, carries no repository content, and cannot change what any query returns: a reader that lied in either direction would change only the wording of a health row, never a locate, search, context, trace, review, or xref answer. Publication is a temp-and-rename with an fsync of the staged file and then of the containing directory, the same shape last_admission.rs beside it and write_generation_marker in crates/kin-daemon/src/state.rs use for the authority head marker. Routing through a shared boundary helper instead was not available: kin-core exposes no public atomic-write path, and config.rs, registry.rs, last_admission.rs, and the daemon's state.rs each open-code their own. Function-scoped rather than whole-file so the rest of the module stays scanned, including the comparison rule, the movement classification, and the cause lookup, and so any newly added filesystem primitive here fails the guard until it is justified.

Host-environment probe and a durable disclosure marker, neither an answer authority. Two classes of pin, checked individually. (1) The host reading: /proc/meminfo is this machine's own memory accounting, read so heavy work can decide whether to start; the cgroup half of the same reading goes through kin_daemon_spawn::cgroup_memory rather than opening /sys/fs/cgroup a second time, and the macOS half is a pair of syscalls with no filesystem access at all. The file names no entity, carries no repository content, and a reader that lied in either direction would change how much work Kin does and never what a locate, search, context, trace, review or xref returns. (2) The refusal record: .kin/memory-pressure holds the most recent piece of heavy work this store's daemon declined and the sentence it declined it with, written by the daemon that decided and read by kin doctor, kin graph status and the MCP envelope, which run later and in other processes. It sits beside the sweep-interruption tally in kin-daemon-spawn and exists for the same reason: the process that made the decision is not the process that has to report it, and a daemon-log WARN reaches nobody. Last writer wins and an unparsable record reads as absent, so it can withhold no answer and produce none. Pinned by exact expression rather than whole-file so the grading rule, the thresholds and the disclosure wording stay scanned, and so any added occurrence fails closed.

Host event ingestion boundary. The excused bodies are the file watcher's admission path: reading a host file or symlink target and its mode so the change can be admitted into the graph as exact tree state, and comparing a host entry against what the graph already holds so an unchanged file is not re-admitted. Reading the working tree is the entire job of an ingestion boundary, and the result is written into graph truth rather than returned as an answer. The remaining two are repository binding, which precedes any graph consult: recognizing a bare git layout, and resolving a path relative to the bound root. The helper that canonicalized a host parent while preserving its leaf moved to kin-index, which is a declared ingestion boundary, so the watcher and this runner decide repository containment by one rule instead of two. The cfg-gated executable-bit helper is the pair that carries a count of two. Function-scoped so the rest of the runner stays scanned. Two further bodies are operational state beside the pid and port files, the same class as the sweep's own enrichment marker in daemon.rs: one records the repository paths this daemon derived entities for and could not have published, the other reads that record back on the next open. Neither reads repository content and neither answers a query. What the record names is decided against graph truth before anything acts on it, which is the point: without it a file whose entities died with the daemon that derived them stays admitted and unqueryable forever (FIR-2606).

Daemon run loop boundary. Two pins are the liveness checks that ask whether this daemon's own repository root and control plane are still present, which is a question about the process rather than about the repository. The rest are the run loop reporting its process id, exiting, and canonicalizing the bound repository root twice while wiring authority into the server. No repository content is read and no query answer derives from any of it. Pinned by expression rather than by function, because the run loop is half this module and exempting its body would leave more unscanned than the primitives justify. The liveness pins first named endpoint_files_missing and control_plane_missing, expressions that stopped existing when a classifier replaced them to verify who owns an endpoint before treating its absence as an eviction notice. Their successors, repository_root_missing and classify_control_plane, were then exempted per function, which excused twenty-four lines to license two expressions. They are pinned again, but on the primitive rather than on a snippet: the two `.exists()` calls are the only filesystem primitive in either body, and a count on the primitive survives the rewording that made the first pins stale while still failing the guard the moment a third appears. Two further pins are the cold sweep's completion marker at <kin_dir>/lsp-enriched-files.json, one read at startup and one write per file finished. It records which files a background enrichment pass has already queried a language server about, so a restart resumes instead of re-sweeping the whole repository, and it is bookkeeping about that pass rather than repository content: no entity, relation or query answer derives from it, and an absent or unreadable marker degrades to a full re-sweep rather than to a wrong answer. It exists because inferring the same fact from the graph failed twice, silently and on the three files the enrichment ticket is about, which is why the sweep now records what it DID instead. Pinned on the primitives with counts, matching the rest of this entry: a third fs call fails the guard. Two further pins are the cold sweep's consecutive-interruption counter at <kin_dir>/lsp-sweep-interruptions, one read when the daemon decides whether to queue a sweep and one write when a sweep ends. It records how many sweeps in a row ended early without enriching anything, so a store whose sweep cannot survive stops being handed another one on every daemon start; one stranger session logged 24 such sweeps against one repository. It is bookkeeping about the pass in exactly the sense the marker above is: no entity, relation or query answer derives from it, and an absent or unreadable counter degrades to the current behaviour of queueing a sweep rather than to a wrong answer. It is a file rather than in-memory state because the loop it guards spans daemon RESTARTS, and a counter that resets on every start cannot see the pattern it exists to detect. Pinned on the primitives with counts like the rest of this entry, so the write pin rises from one to two and the read is pinned on read_to_string rather than read: a third write or a second read_to_string fails the guard. Three further pins are the cold sweep's in-flight record at <kin_dir>/lsp-sweep-in-flight, one write when a sweep begins, one removal when it reaches its end, and one existence probe with its removal on the next daemon start. Everything a sweep makes durable happens after its last file, so a process that ends mid-sweep reaches none of it and the store keeps no trace that a sweep ever ran: a killed sweep and a sweep that never started read the same, which is what made the interruption counter above blind to the very loop it guards. This record is the difference, and it is bookkeeping about the pass in exactly the sense the two above are. No entity, relation or query answer derives from it, and an absent or unreadable record degrades to today's behaviour of queueing a sweep rather than to a wrong answer. It is a file rather than in-memory state for the same reason the counter is, because the fact it carries is only ever read by a LATER process. Pinned on the primitives with counts like the rest of this entry, so the write pin rises from two to three, the existence pin from two to three, and removal is pinned at two: a fourth write, a fourth probe or a third removal fails the guard. The interruption tally's own read and write moved down to `kin-daemon-spawn` once `kin graph status`, `kin doctor` and the MCP envelope had to answer the same question about it, so this module keeps the tally's callers and none of its IO: the write pin falls back from three to two and the read pin is gone entirely, which means a reintroduced read here fails the guard rather than passing under an inherited count. A third write pin is the same completion marker being RETIRED for a file a reconcile just changed. Nothing removed an entry before, so a file swept once was skipped by every later sweep for the life of the store however far its declarations had moved, which is what made the FIR-2598 edge loss permanent and what let `kin daemon sweep` report "enriched 37/37 files" in 518 ms over 37 files it skipped. The primitive is the same rewrite of the same bookkeeping file the per-sweep write above performs, on the same terms: no entity, relation or query answer derives from it, and a failed rewrite degrades to a re-sweep rather than to a wrong answer. The write pin rises from two to three; a fourth fails the guard.

Daemon process entry point. Neither class reads repository content nor answers a query. Pinned by expression with exact counts rather than by function, because the four functions involved are most of this binary and exempting their bodies would leave more unscanned than the primitives justify.

Process liveness boundary with zero answer-authority surface. This module publishes one fact about the daemon process, that it currently has a write transaction open, which phase is running, and when it last beat, into .kin/daemon.transaction, and reads that file back so the supervisor's reaper can tell a busy daemon from a wedged one. It exists because the reaper's only other liveness question is GET /health, which a daemon doing synchronous commit work on a runtime worker cannot answer, so the guard that refuses to reap a working daemon could not fire for the one state it protects; a 172-second commit was SIGKILLed as a result. The marker's file reads and writes now live in kin-daemon-spawn, which both the daemon and the CLI depend on, so a lost commit reply can be classified from the same record the reaper reads; that crate's entry pins them. What remains here is this process's own pid, recorded into the marker so a reader can tell whether the daemon that opened it is still alive. Nothing in it reaches repository content, and it can only withhold a kill, never produce, rank, fill, or repair an answer to locate, search, context, trace, review, xref, or rename. Pinned by exact expression so any newly added filesystem primitive in this module fails the guard until it is re-justified.

kin-agent is a CLIENT of graph authority, never a source of it. It reaches Kin only through the MCP server over stdio, so every tool result it hands a model comes from the graph, and it deliberately ships no file-read, file-search or shell tool for a model to call. The filesystem and subprocess touches here are the two explicit boundaries the zero-file-search rule allows: materializing an edit the model asked for, and writing the run's own transcript. This module is the write boundary. `edit_file` reads the one file it is about to change so a find-and-replace can be exact and can refuse an ambiguous match, and `write_file` writes the one file it was given; both resolve the path inside the repository first and refuse any escape. Neither answers a question: the model has already been told where the code is by `mcp__kin__semantic_locate` and what it says by `mcp__kin__get_entity_source`, and nothing derived from these reads reaches a tool result. Pinned rather than whole-file so a newly added filesystem primitive in this module fails the guard, which is exactly what should happen if anyone ever adds a read or search tool to the belt.
